opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was difficult because vLLM was never supposed to be about a company. It started as an academic open-source project, and the thing that made it work was that everyone trusted it was neutral. Hardware vendors, model labs, cloud providers, startups: they all contributed because no single party owned it. The moment you say "we're starting a company around this," people naturally ask whether the project will now serve the company's interests instead of the community's. That trust took years to build, and I was very afraid of damaging it.

The second part was personal. I came from a research background. I enjoyed going deep on technical problems like compilation, `torch.compile` integration, and making the system cleaner. Running a company means hiring, fundraising, talking to customers, and making trade-offs that aren't purely technical. I had to ask myself whether that was really what I wanted to spend my time on, or whether I'd be happier staying a core maintainer and researcher.

Third, there's the open-source business model problem. Everyone knows the story: you build something great and free, and then the large clouds can take it and run it at scale better than you can. So you have to think hard about where a company actually adds value without closing things off or holding features back. I didn't want to become the kind of company that slowly moves the good stuff into a proprietary edition.

What eventually changed my mind was seeing that the project's needs had outgrown what volunteers and grad students could sustain. vLLM was running in production at huge scale, models were changing every few weeks, and new hardware kept arriving. Someone had to take long-term responsibility for maintenance, testing, and release quality, full-time and with real resources. I came to see a company as a way to protect the open-source project rather than exploit it, as long as we committed clearly to keeping the core open and the governance community-driven. But getting to that conclusion took a lot of sleepless nights.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a research and technical role—working on compilation and system improvements—with the company responsibilities of hiring, fundraising, serving customers, and making trade-offs.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was difficult because it meant giving up a lot of things I had taken for granted about my own path. I was still at Tsinghua finishing my PhD, and the plan in my head had always been quite academic: write papers, maybe do a postdoc, stay close to research. vLLM started for me as a contribution on the side. I was fixing bugs, working on distributed inference, the torch.compile integration, things like that. It was open source, it was fun, and it didn't require me to make any big life decision.

But as the project grew, I started to see a tension that open source alone couldn't resolve. vLLM became infrastructure. Companies were running it in production, hardware vendors wanted their chips supported, users expected releases to be stable, security issues to be handled, performance to keep up with every new model. That kind of work isn't glamorous. It doesn't produce papers. And it's very hard to sustain with volunteers and a handful of people funded by university labs or by their employers' goodwill. I watched maintainers burn out. I felt it myself.

So the question became: if this project matters, who is responsible for it long term? And the uncomfortable answer was that someone has to build an organization around it, with real funding and real full-time people. Once I accepted that, the next question was whether that someone should be me, and that was the hard part. I am an engineer and a researcher by temperament. I had never managed a budget, never hired, never thought about business models. There was a real fear that founding a company would pull me away from the code, which is the thing I actually love.

There was also the open source concern. The moment you put a company next to a community project, people start asking whether the company will capture it. I care a lot about vLLM staying genuinely neutral, with contributors from many companies and many hardware ecosystems. I had to think carefully about how to structure things so that the company serves the project rather than the other way around. We spent a lot of time talking with the Berkeley folks and the broader community about that before committing.

And finally, there was just the personal weight of it. You are asking people to leave good jobs and join you, you are asking investors to trust you, and you are doing it in a field where everything changes every three months. I went back and forth for a long time. In the end what tipped me was realizing that not deciding was also a decision, and that if I waited for the perfect moment, the project would either stall or be shaped by someone whose priorities I didn't share. So I decided it was better to take the responsibility myself, even knowing I would have to learn most of it on the job.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving from familiar engineering and research work to building an organization and taking responsibility for vLLM’s long-term support, including unfamiliar duties like budgeting, hiring, and business models.

astra-6.text:
I think the hardest part was deciding what responsibility I wanted to take on. Supporting vLLM technically is one thing; founding a company means committing to customers, employees, and all the work needed to keep the company running. It changes how you spend your time.

And there’s a tension you have to think through: how do you build a sustainable business while keeping the open-source project useful to the whole community? A company can give you resources to support the project, but you have to be thoughtful about how those two things fit together. That made it a much bigger decision than simply wanting to keep working on vLLM.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts supporting vLLM technically with taking on the responsibilities of founding and running a company, including customers, employees, and ongoing operations.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the difficult part was figuring out whether starting a company was really the right way to support the project. With an open-source project, you want to make it useful for everyone. A company has to find customers, generate revenue, and make commitments to them. Those goals can align, but they don’t automatically align.

I also enjoyed the technical work. Starting a company means taking on a very different set of responsibilities—hiring, fundraising, and making decisions that affect other people’s livelihoods. So it wasn’t just, “Do I believe in vLLM?” It was, “Is this the right structure to help it grow, and am I ready to take on that responsibility?”

r001.rationale: The response contrasts enjoying technical work with taking on company responsibilities such as hiring, fundraising, and decisions affecting livelihoods, conveying the shift from technical work to responsibility for the company’s development.
